title: Clara's Unexpected Sparkle
markdown:
Clara the dormouse was a creature of exceptional order. Her whiskers did not merely twitch; they vibrated with the joy of a perfectly alphabetized hymn book. She was Choir Librarian for the Meadowbrook Annual Awards Supper, the evening that conferred the Most Diligent Daffodil for outstanding contributions to community merriment. Clara had her sights on that honour. She had spent weeks polishing the music sheets until they gleamed, ensuring every note sat in its rightful place. In her estimation it was a triumph of organization. She even kept a special velvet cushion for the conductor’s baton.

The plan is still excellent. Reality is simply being overfamiliar.

Her older sister, Yara the mole, was a study in earthy pragmatism. Where Clara saw a symphony of Dewey Decimal, Yara saw the potential for a root-bound flowerbed. Yara’s paws were always smudged with soil. “Clara, darling,” Yara would rumble, “have you remembered to water the potted plants for the hall? They look a bit droopy. And did you check if the fairy lights are properly tangled? Last year was a fright.” Clara would pat a music stand. “They’re perfectly hydrated with anticipation. And the lights are a very delicate work in progress.”

The night before the supper, Meadowbrook Community Hall buzzed with a frantic energy Clara found unsettling. Bunting drooped from the rafters like sleepy caterpillars. Tablecloths made fabric mountains. And the choir’s music — Clara’s precious organized music — was in utter disarray. She had been so focused on immaculate spines and crisp pages that she had forgotten the main program. Panic gnawed at her paws.

“Oh, dearie me,” she squeaked. “It’s all jumbled. The finale music is not where it should be.” She pictured the rousing medley that always made whiskers twitch, and felt a cold dread.

Yara arrived with a wheelbarrow of dahlias and a large sack of earthworms. “Jumbled? Not quite the Dewey Decimal system we discussed for floral arrangements.” She nudged a precarious stack of sheet music. “Looks as if a startled squirrel redecorated with paper confetti.”

Clara’s paws fluttered. “I made a note for you, Yara. To remind me about the grand finale sheet, the one with the extra flourish. I put it somewhere. I was going to give it to you first thing.” She rummaged through programmes. “Ah. Here.”

She pulled out a crumpled scrap, slightly damp from dandelion tea, that she had accidentally tucked into the main program booklet. It had landed on the guest list.

The note, in Clara’s neat hand, read: Yara, darling sister, Remember: The plan is still excellent. Reality is simply being overfamiliar. And for the finale — make it HUGE. Surprise them.

A hush fell. Old Mr. Fitzwilliam, a badger, paused his buffing of a trophy. Mrs. Higgins, a rabbit, peered over her spectacles. The air crackled.

Clara’s fur flushed crimson. “That was private. About the finale.” The Daffodil award seemed to crumble.

Yara surveyed the scene with a low chuckle. “That’s quite the philosophy for our grand finale.”

Mr. Fitzwilliam adjusted his monocle. “Reality is simply being overfamiliar. Fascinating. Perhaps that’s why my garden gnomes seem so bored this year.”

Mrs. Higgins clapped. “A surprise for the finale. I always suspected there was more to Clara’s music than meets the ear.”

Clara’s private note had become a public declaration. Everyone took it as profound wisdom.

“It wasn’t meant to be a public announcement,” Clara wailed, burying her face. “It was a reminder about the extra sparkle. A little something unexpected.”

Yara nudged her. “And isn’t that wonderful? You were so worried about perfect order you forgot that unexpected sparks are what make things shine. Mr. Fitzwilliam is contemplating the ennui of garden ornaments, and Mrs. Higgins is vibrating for a huge finale.”

Young Pip the field mouse piped up. “I could help with the flourish. I’m good at wiggling my tail really fast. I can make it look like a shooting star.” Pwyll the badger stomped forward. “If it’s a huge surprise, it needs a huge backdrop. Something with stars. I’ve got excellent luminous paints.”

Clara looked around, bewildered. A tiny seed of hope sprouted. The embarrassing note had unlocked everyone else’s creativity.

As the choir’s opening number filled the hall, Clara watched from the wings, her heart fluttery with anticipation rather than dread. The huge surprise involved Pip’s tail-wiggling galaxy on the ceiling and Pwyll’s painted moonlit meadow. Clara’s music was still meticulously organized, but now it belonged to something larger.

When the last note faded and the hall erupted, Clara stood beside Yara. The Daffodil was not on her mind. She watched the shared smiles of a job that had been better for a little unexpected chaos.

“The plan is still excellent,” Yara whispered, squeezing Clara’s paw. “Reality is simply being overfamiliar.”

Clara nodded, her whiskers finally still. The hall smelled of dahlias and luminous paint. The baton cushion sat unused, and nobody missed it.
